newsitem.title: USA: Two guilty of manslaughter in U.S. exorcism death.
newsitem.headline: Two guilty of manslaughter in U.S. exorcism death.

text.p: The husband of a Korean woman who was pummeled to death during an exorcism, and the missionary who led the ritual, were found guilty of involuntary manslaughter by a judge on Wednesday.
Judge James Albracht turned down a prosecution request to convict the men of second degree murder.
"This is a tragedy of Shakespearean magnitude. These defendants were at all times acting in conscience and good faith of healing the victim," he said.

During the three-week, non-jury trial, Albracht heard that the exorcism was performed last July by Jae Whoa Chung, 44, and Sung Soo Choi, 42, and a third man to "cast out demons" from Chung's 53-year-old wife, Kyung Jae Chung, who died of internal injuries following her ordeal.
The Chungs, who ran a Christian school in Bangladesh, and Choi, an underground Christian missionary in China, were in Los Angeles for a prayer meeting when the exorcism took place.
A third defendant, Jin Hyun Choi, 47, a deacon at a local Presbyterian church, earlier pleaded guilty to involuntary manslaughter.

During often emotional testimony, Albracht heard that the exorcism began in a house in the Koreatown section of Los Angeles and moved to a condominium in the Century City area where the woman died of her injuries.

The exorcism ceremony, known as "ansu kido" began with ritual prayers and laying on of hands. Later, the men began slapping the woman's face and pinned down her arms so they could apply pressure to her abdomen to force the demons out, according to trial testimony.

Jin Hyn Choi testified that he and the other two men took turns "stomping" on the victim's chest until they noticed that her chest had "dipped." He said the Century City part of the exorcism, the most violent, lasted five hours.
An autopsy report said Kyung Jae Chung suffered "excruciatingly painful" injuries and looked as if she had been "run over by a car."
But Judge Albracht found that the men, misguided as they were, "did not act in conscious disregard for life."

One of the men's defence lawyers, James Barnes, told reporters outside the court, "We feel gratified the judge was sensitive to the fact that our clients ... were involved in what they believed was a religious healing ceremony.
"They were very, very concerned about Mrs Chung's well-being and wanted to expel this demon that she had suffered from for 27 years."
All three men are to be sentenced later.
